title: Pipeline stage timing surgeon notes
content:
Purpose:
This note captures an end-to-end profiling pass (distributed traces + host counters) focused on p50/p95/p99 breakdowns across pipeline stages. Objective is to record current observations, hypothesize root causes for tail latency, and propose quick experiments/mitigations to shrink p95/p99 for both short and long requests.

Context and test harness:
- Model used: redwood-large-v1 (fp16 runtime path) on dedicated GPU nodes (A100x1).
- Traffic profile simulated: production-like mix (70% short prompts, 30% long generation).
- Trace capture: OpenTelemetry spans emitted from edge LB -> auth -> router -> predictor -> model-worker -> postprocess. Sampling: 10% random sampling, with an extra 1000 tail traces (p99-candidate) captured via adaptive sampling on requests with >1s latency.
- Host counters: nvidia-smi sampling (100ms), dstat, per-process Python GC logs, kernel preemption traces (ftrace), and nvlink bandwidth counters.
- Run window: 2025-02-18 09:00–12:00 PST, steady-state load, n=2500 total requests analyzed.

Summary numbers (overall E2E observed):
1) Short prompt scenario (50 tokens input, synthetic no-embedding, single-shot gen of 16 tokens): n=1750
   - E2E p50: 48 ms
   - E2E p95: 94 ms
   - E2E p99: 178 ms

   Per-stage median (p50) breakdown (ms):
   - Ingress (LB + TLS handshake amortized): 6 ms
   - Auth/Quota check: 2 ms
   - Router dispatch + policy: 3 ms
   - Tokenization: 5 ms
   - Batch formation / queuing (small-batch): 2 ms
   - Model forward (kernel exec, memory ops): 24 ms
   - KV cache lookup/merge: 2 ms
   - Decoding & token selection: 3 ms
   - Response marshal + gzip: 2 ms
   - Streaming flush: 1 ms

   Tail behavior (p95/p99) contributors (observed):
   - p95: model forward increases to ~110 ms for stragglers (single-host scheduling jitter and kernel warmup for rare quantized path).
   - p99: additional 60–120 ms often due to synchronous disk activity on model-worker host (checkpoint read on cold worker) or occasional Python GC pause during response serialization (GC pause samples match ~3% of p99 traces).

2) Long prompt scenario (1024 tokens context, avg generation 512 tokens): n=750
   - E2E p50: 1,240 ms
   - E2E p95: 2,820 ms
   - E2E p99: 5,360 ms

   Per-stage median (p50) breakdown (ms):
   - Ingress: 10 ms
   - Auth: 2 ms
   - Router: 4 ms
   - Tokenization (large context): 28 ms
   - Batch formation / queuing: 12 ms (batching window + waiting for combine)
   - Model-forward total (autoregressive steps): 1,150 ms
       - Kernel exec time (summed): ~980 ms
       - KV cache standby/merge: ~35 ms
       - Inter-step host overhead (kernel launch latency, stream sync): ~135 ms
   - Decoding overhead: 20 ms
   - Postprocess + attach metadata: 10 ms
   - Streaming flush (chunks): 8 ms

   Tail observations (p95/p99):
   - p95: model-forward variance dominates. For many p95 traces we saw a single kernel execution 2–4x slower due to mixed-device data movement (NVLink congestion in multi-GPU hosts used for other workloads).
   - p99: two main causes seen repeatedly in traces:
       1) Host preemption -> process being moved or stalled (hypervisor scheduling) causing 500–1200 ms holes mid-generation.
       2) Kernel fallback: when the primary optimized kernel was not selected (memory layout mismatch), runtime fell back to a generic slower kernel adding 300–1500 ms for that step.

Evidence from traces and counters:
- Correlated traces with nvidia-smi: spikes in PCIe utilization and transient NVLink bandwidth saturation align with top p95 traces.
- ftrace samples show occasional syscall spikes (fsync, read) in 8% of p99 traces—points to unexpected disk IO in hot path (checkpoint reloads or model quant table loads).
- Python-level logs: GC \"stop-the-world\" events found in 3% of p99 short traces. These correlate with large response objects being built (debug metadata enabled).
- Router metrics: a handful of maladaptive routing decisions pushed requests to nodes with older kernel caches (cold-start kernels) causing extra 120–400 ms while kernels JIT/compiled.

Key hypotheses (ranked):
1) Kernel selection and cold kernel paths are the biggest contributor for long-tail model-forward latency (especially for long requests with rare sequence lengths or quantization variants).
2) Host-level preemption and noisy neighbors (multi-tenant GPU hosts) cause the largest single spikes at p99.
3) Synchronous disk IO and on-demand KV-cache misses are second-order but actionable (we saw fsync/read in traces).
4) Python GC + synchronous serialization can push short requests into p99 — avoid heavyweight debug-only metadata in production hot path.

Quick mitigations to try (short-middle-run):
- Add a kernel-warmup pass during worker startup for the most common sequence lengths/quant variants. Measure delta by re-running trace harness.
- Cap max batch wait window to 5ms for small-request routes (cut queuing tail).
- Disable heavy debug metadata generation in production hot path; move to async logger.
- Pre-warm KV cache on worker cold start; ensure KV entries for common prefixes live in memory.
- Mark critical model-serving VMs as \"predictor-priority\" (isolate from batch training workloads) to avoid hypervisor-level preemption on busiest nodes.

Longer-run changes / experiments:
- Add per-kernel compile metrics in runtime telemetry and emit a \"kernel_fallback\" span tag so traces directly show fallback cases.
- Implement a lightweight in-memory journal to replace sync disk reads in hot path (eliminate observed fsynces).
- Run an A/B test: quantized variant (int8) for short prompts vs fp16 baseline to measure token latency and p99 improvements (expected: ~20–40% model-forward latency reduction on short requests).
- Evaluate preemptible-host scheduling: reassign inference hosts to single-tenant pool for VIP customers to see p99 improvement.

Experiment plan (next 2 weeks):
1) Kernel warmup script rollout to 10% of workers; collect traces (target: reduce kernel-fallback p99 occurrences by 70%). Owner: Michael Chen. ETA: 3 days.
2) Short-route batch window change (5ms) in Canary for hosted API small requests; measure p95/p99 over 48h. Owner: Priya Nair. ETA: 2 days.
3) Disable debug metadata and switch to async logging on worker hot path; remeasure short-request p99. Owner: Daniela Ruiz. ETA: 1 day.
4) Run synthetic noise experiment to reproduce host-preemption p99: schedule background CPU/GPU noise on a subset and observe tail. Owner: Luca Moretti. ETA: 4 days.

Open questions / observations to follow up:
- How frequently do different sequence lengths map to fallback kernels? Need a histogram of (seq_len, kernel_id) from runtime for two weeks.
- Are our autoscaler decisions ever spinning up cold workers that do heavy disk pulls mid-traffic? Add hooks to pause scale-up until warmup completes.
- Can we get hypervisor-level scheduling telemetry from cloud provider to validate preemption hypothesis?

Appendix: quick trace exemplar (short p99) — condensed span list (times in ms):
- ingress: 6
- auth: 2
- router: 3
- tokenization: 5
- batch-wait: 1
- model-forward (step 1): 105  <-- kernel fallback observed here
- decode: 3
- serialize: 28  <-- Python GC and metadata attach
- e2e total: 179

Notes to self: keep this doc as a living scratchpad. After each experiment paste delta numbers and links to follow-up traces. Use this to build a short RCA for the next "serving-runtime" weekly sync if mitigations move the needle.

References and helpers:
- tracing query: service=worker and span.operation=model-forward and tag:kernel_fallback=true -> view traces for last 7d
- perf dashboards: observability/latency/p95-by-route (use date filter 2025-02-18 to 2025-02-24)
- relevant PR: github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/612 (batcher: reduce max-coalesce-window)

End of note.
